followUps.question: What problems does horizontal scaling introduce?
followUps.answer: Horizontal scaling introduces distributed systems complexity: data consistency, session management, distributed caching, service discovery, and debugging across multiple servers.
followUps.interviewPitch: Horizontal scaling introduces distributed system complexities, primarily around State Management and Data Consistency. If you have 5 servers, you can no longer store user sessions or uploaded files on the server's local hard drive (because the load balancer might send the user to a different server next time). You must externalize state using Redis or JWTs, and externalize file storage using AWS S3. It also requires distributed databases, bringing in the complexities of the CAP Theorem.
followUps.explanation:
**🧠 The Shared Brain Problem:**
Imagine one Chef making pizzas. He remembers that Table 4 is allergic to peanuts (Local State). It's easy.

Now you horizontally scale to 5 Chefs. 
Chef A takes the order from Table 4 and learns about the allergy. He saves it in his own brain. 
Five minutes later, Table 4 asks Chef B for some bread. Chef B has no idea they are allergic to peanuts! He gives them peanut bread!

**The Solution:** You have to buy a giant whiteboard (Redis Cache) and put it in the middle of the kitchen. ALL chefs must write down and read allergies from the shared whiteboard.
followUps.whyAsked: Tests if you understand the real-world trade-offs beyond just 'add more servers'.
mistakes: Thinking horizontal scaling is free of complexity — it's a major architecture shift.
Forgetting the database becomes the bottleneck when app servers scale but the DB doesn't.
followUps.diagram:
flowchart TD
    subgraph Local State (Fails on Scale!)
    S1[Server A] --> M1[(Local RAM: Bob is logged in)]
    S2[Server B] --> M2[(Local RAM: Who is Bob?)]
    end
    
    subgraph External State (Scalable!)
    S3[Server A] --> Redis[(Shared Redis Cache)]
    S4[Server B] --> Redis
    end

    style Redis fill:#ccffcc,stroke:#00cc00

followUps.question: What are Sticky Sessions (Session Affinity)?
followUps.answer: A load balancer sits in front of multiple servers and distributes incoming requests across them using algorithms like round-robin or least connections.
followUps.interviewPitch: Sticky Sessions (Session Affinity) is a load balancer configuration that forces all requests from a specific user to always be routed to the exact same server they originally connected to. While this solves the problem of local session state in legacy applications, it is considered an anti-pattern in modern System Design because it ruins the even distribution of the load balancer and completely breaks auto-scaling and server failovers.
followUps.explanation:
**🪑 The Assigned Seating Analogy:**
• **Standard Load Balancing:** Every time you go to the cafeteria, the manager points you to the shortest line. You get your food fast.
• **Sticky Sessions:** The manager says, "You went to Register 4 yesterday, so you MUST go to Register 4 today." Even if Register 4 has a line of 100 people, and Register 3 is completely empty, you are forced to wait. Worse, if the cashier at Register 4 goes home sick (Server Crash), you get kicked out of the cafeteria (Logged Out).
followUps.whyAsked: Tests if you understand how traffic distribution works in a scaled system.
mistakes: Thinking load balancers only do round-robin — there are many algorithms for different needs.
Forgetting that the load balancer itself can be a SPOF — use redundant LBs or cloud-managed ones.
followUps.diagram:
flowchart LR
    U1[User Bob] -->|Logs In| LB[Load Balancer]
    LB -->|Creates Sticky Cookie| S1[Server A]
    
    U1 -->|Next Request| LB
    LB -.->|Forces routing| S1
    
    Note over S1: If Server A crashes, Bob loses his session!
